utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good afternoon, everybody. May we hear the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances, please. The OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Nicholas Koumjian, assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we turn to today's witness, I have to inform the parties on the following -- it was my intention to have a hearing also the 10th of July, but I was informed via the legal officer that this would cause some problems with the Defence. And the Defence is not in town at that day? Or can we hear the reason, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One of the reasons is that the Defence is not in the town on that day. Of course, it could be rescheduled, but at the same time, we have scheduled a visit by the mother of Mr. Stakic with her son. And we usually leave the apartment when the family of Mr. Stakic comes to Den Haag, so it should be rescheduled twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If there are no objections by the OTP, I think good cause is shown not to hear this case on this date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't raise any matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, as regards Friday, 19th of July, unfortunately, we can't have a hearing this Friday because we have hearings in four other cases before Trial Chamber II. This will be in Obrenovic, Mrdja, Mrksic, and one other case. We'll send out the scheduling order later. But unfortunately, it's not possible to have any courtroom for these purposes before August 2. So therefore, we had to arrange this. As regards August 1 and August 2, until now under the provision, provisional only, we try to find out what is possible to have the hearing on both days in the morning, if necessary. But we'll hear about this later. Finally, what about the motion on Rule 95. The Defence indicated that they would be prepared to file a new motion by today. Is it already prepared?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. John Ostojic, on behalf of the Defence. I did review the transcript and the Court's comments and consulted with Mr. Lukic, and this morning briefly with my learned friend, Ms. Korner, we discussed that we have not completed the motion in full, and we're waiting to get dates which are necessary from a certain letter in connection with part of our motion. But we have accepted what the Court said in connection with the VWS, and will act accordingly. So we'll expect to have that filed no later than Wednesday and present it to the Court on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. I would appreciate if it could be filed and, in addition, be read out in the courtroom for expeditious decision on this motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The report the parties received in addition, the decision of the Appeals Chamber as regards the identification, so there are any comments to make on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Such comments as I might have are not particularly helpful, Your Honour. We have received the decision, in fact, I was going to raise it with Your Honour today, as to how Your Honour wants us to proceed from here on in. In other words, the actual mechanics of holding this identification parade. As I understood it, at one stage, Your Honours were suggesting that the identification parade should be held in Court. I don't know whether that's still Your Honours' intention. Can I point out to a number of practical difficulties in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the burden of proof and the burden how to conduct this de lege artis is with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Can I put it this way: I don't know what Your Honour's practice in Your Honour's jurisdiction is, but certainly in our jurisdiction identification parades would be held in police stations. That applies equally to -- not in a court. And the people selected for the parade would be general members of the public. Now that obviously isn't going to apply, for one thing, there's no police station. Two, I'm not sure we can drag general members of the public here. Also, the Defence would have the right to object to the people selected. I mean, as a process, it's quite a long process. So that's why I'm asking whether Your Honours want it done in Court in front of Your Honours or whether Your Honours want it done outside the Court either in the Detention Unit where arrangements will have to be made with those who run the unit and arrangements will have to be made for, I think Your Honour said, five -- four similar people to be brought there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Four additional, yes. Yes, we're working on the basis of the best possible evidence. And of course, the best possible evidence would be to see the immediate reaction of the witness immediately in front of us. And therefore, the most favourable solution would be, without any doubt, to have five persons sitting here in the courtroom. And I think it couldn't be too much a problem -- I know the problems to recruit people from the street, as is done usually in our home countries. But why not try to find these people amongst the staff members of this Tribunal. I think this could be a solution. But to be honest, I want to leave the utmost discretion, of course, to the Prosecutor. And when selecting these persons, of course, it's only fair to discuss this with the Defence in preparation whether or not the Defence has any objections on the outcome of this selection. But I think it would be fair if, for example, the OTP presents, let's say, seven persons, and you agree on four persons together with the Defence. This could be a solution, but I want to leave it absolutely to the parties to decide this. But I believe it could be done, and it would facilitate the proceedings directly in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, I understand that Your Honour would prefer that the identification takes place for the first time in the courtroom with people who look similar to Dr. Stakic sitting somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Space enough, even in our shoebox.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I should point out that Dr. Stakic is -- perhaps not the easiest person to find similarity to, given his beard and his hair line, if I can put it that way. But we'll see what we can do. Your Honour, the next point is I understand the matter Your Honour said should there not only be an identification parade of what he looks like now, but Your Honour wants the photo board as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It was the intention of the OTP to provide the photo board, and what we said until now was that from our point of view, there is no obstacle that in addition, the attempt is made to recognise a person on the basis of a photo board. And you prepared this photo board. There were, if I remember correctly, the Defence had some objections against the one or other photograph shown on this board. But once again, this has to be settled amongst the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to confirm. That's as he looked like ten years ago when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, we'll see what we can arrange obviously. I think it's anticipated the witness will be called towards the end of the month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of July, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. And this brings me to the final point: What about the estimated length of the Prosecutor's case from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've reprepared a list of how long we anticipate the remaining witnesses will take. Your Honour, it's our view that the case will run roughly to mid-September, with the break. Perhaps the beginning of the third week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We may have this writing that we can follow the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've updated the estimates for those 65 ter if we can hand those in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Excellent. Could the usher be so kind and give one, first, for the Defence of course, and then to the Judges. Thank you. Thank you for this preparation, because we have to find out when to continue with the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think we were -- our understanding was that it would be recommenced on the 26th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Immediately after the Court recess, indeed. And then until mid-September. This was the common understanding. If nothing happens in the meantime not foreseeable, probably there will be some difficulties as regards interpretation after the summer break. But it's not yet ripe for discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, then may I return finally before the witness comes in if I may, there was a discussion I think in the Status Conference, a discussion about handwriting. And I think Your Honours were going to return to the matter. I don't know whether -- in the sense that we can't carry out a handwriting comparison unless we have samples of handwriting to compare it with. And I think Mr. Koumjian raised this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You received the two orders of this Chamber on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. We haven't seen any orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: They were filed. We have already received it in return, so please, wait until --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hadn't appreciated Your Honours had filed orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It was already --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was filed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On Friday. It hasn't reached us yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Probably we can come back later today to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll attempt to get the orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we should proceed as soon as possible with the cross-examination. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. The reason why -- I completely forgot, before the witness comes back, when he left last week, he gave to VWS, who passed it on to us, a document. It is an original of -- we did a draft translation. I think Your Honours were given a copy, of a letter removing somebody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From Celpak?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it Celpak in the first line?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then we have it before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour. Your Honour, we gave it to the Defence. Clearly because he's been giving evidence, nobody's spoken to him about it. I don't know where it comes from, how he got it, or what made him produce it. I'm just asking for Your Honours' assistance or guidance as to how it should be dealt with, whether Your Honours would wish me to reopen examination-in-chief with him to deal with this document or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it would be the most appropriate way in this party procedure, and just before we really start with the witness, I wanted to ask the parties: When some issues will be discussed emanating from the letter I read out during the last hearing, and all the question in this context, let us know beforehand, and I think we have to go for good reasons then in closed session again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the letter that Your Honour read into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: About the assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well Your Honour, at the end of cross-examination, I was going to raise various matters about the cross-examination in any event, basically to say I'm not at all clear what case, if any, is being put to this witness at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Only that we are clear, do you agree that we just for a few minutes restart, on the basis of this document, with the examination-in-chief? It's an interruption once again of your cross-examination. Therefore, I have to ask you for your permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That would be fine by us. My only question is, I'm not sure if we have the document that counsel is referring to. So if we may have an extra copy of it, we appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we've done is we've done a colour copy for Your Honours and one for the Defence. Can I ask, perhaps, that what is exhibited in this case, Your Honours of course and the Defence can look at the original, but rather than making the original an exhibit, to make one of the colour copies an exhibit because it will be needed for the Brdjanin/Talic trial at a later stage. And once it becomes an exhibit here, it becomes quite complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the meantime, when this document is distributed, what about our request for colour copies?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think we have got a number of colour copies for Your Honours of the documents you requested. Your Honour, we've copied sets of all the colour copies. One is for Your Honours, one is for the registry, and one is for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The colour copies, one for the Defence, one for the registry, and one for the Judges. That's the first batch, Your Honour. More are coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we agree that we start a new binder including these colour copies, and it's my understanding you tender this into evidence. Any objections against the admission into evidence of these colour copies? I think they have additional probative value to that what we had in the past.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just wonder whether they shouldn't be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Concentrated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whether they shouldn't be -- because they are already exhibited all these document, whether they shouldn't become a version of the actual exhibit numbers they've got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can do it this way, add these to the former documents under -1. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The colour copies will be admitted into evidence under the number of the exhibit already admitted into evidence, only, in addition, -1 to the number they have already. And then finally, it is your intention to tender the copy of the document we have now before us in colour copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As an exhibit, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not as a colour copy, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the next available number will be, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So, this will be Exhibit S182.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence as S182B, and the draft translation, S182A. Anything else to be settled before we start? I can see nothing. Then please, may the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good to see you back in The Hague. Please be seated. I don't want to start without recalling that of course, even there was a longer break, all that what you have to say today and tomorrow, the same rules apply. And you are still acting under your solemn declaration. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I do. And I accept this, just as I did when I made the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. As evidently out of the blue, a document was tendered, we start for a short moment with the examination-in-chief. Please, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, before you left, you handed to the victims and witnesses service a document. Could you have a look, please, at this document.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the document I submitted through the assistant. I sent it from the airport in Amsterdam. This is a decision dismissing from work an employee who was not an ethnic Serb and who was an ordinary worker. If the Court wishes, I can read out what is written in the document. And if the Court wishes, I can also explain how I came into possession of this document and why I submitted it to you in the way that I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This document bears the heading "The Celpak Cellulose and Paper Factory, PO Prijedor. Director of the sector for personnel, legal, and general administration." The document bears the number 466. And the date, the 16th of October, 1992. Further, it says: "Pursuant to an order of the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipality number 001-023-49/92, of the 2nd of July, 1992, I hereby issue the following decision on the termination of employment: "One, to the worker (redacted), working at the post of first assistant --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are not aware of this term.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- "preparation of acid. His employment is terminated because of his participation in the armed rebellion in the Municipality of Prijedor on the 2nd of July, 1992." Then there follows an explanation of reasons, a statement of reasons. "By the order of the Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Prijedor, number 01-023-49/92, of the 2nd of July, all organisations were ordered, if they had employees who took part in the armed rebellion and who are now in one of the refugee camps of Omarska or Keraterm, to terminate their employment. "Acting in accordance with the above-mentioned order, and pursuant to the letter received from the public security station number 11-12-26, of the 16th of July, 1992, on the register of such persons, the decision mentioned in the disposition of this decision was reached." And then, in the left hand bottom corner, it says: "Delivered to" and there is a list of four addresses. "One, the above-named. Two, the financial department for the payroll. Three, to EJ, who is the head of a unit." I assume it's the energy unit, but I'm not sure. "And four: "To the employment department." And the signature is that of the director of the sector for legal, personnel and administrative affairs, Zeljko Skondric, a graduate lawyer. And there is a handwritten signature over the typed name, and the stamp of the Celpak factory. There is nothing on the other side. There is only a handwritten telephone number on the other side. The way I came into possession of this document is as follows: When I testified before the Tribunal two years ago, I don't know the exact date, a gentleman called (redacted) [Realtime transcript read in error (redacted)] was also before the Tribunal. And on completing our obligations to the Tribunal, just as we were setting out to go home, he told me that he had this document with him, and that he had forgotten to give it to the investigators. He asked me to do this. I took the piece of paper from him. I didn't study it in detail. I only saw that it was a decision on dismissal from work, and I forgot to hand over the document. The document was in a pocket inside my leather bag. I remember that (redacted) (redacted) then told me how he had received this document, but now I'm not so sure about it any more. Either it was handed to his wife, who went to the company, or to him personally. I'm not sure about that any more. But this person exists, and this information can easily be checked. At the airport in Amsterdam, while we were waiting for our flight, I put my plane ticket and some other papers in this pocket inside my bag, and Mr. Greg, who was the assistant accompanying us to the airport saw this. I felt inside the pocket, and I discovered this piece of paper, and then I wrote several sentences on a blank sheet of paper. And I asked Greg to deliver this to the Tribunal if he could. He was present when I was writing this note, and I gave this document and the note into his hands and asked him to deliver it if possible to see if it could be of use to the Court. But anyway, two years ago, I undertook to do this, and I really forgot. So in this way, I have carried out my promise to this gentleman, and I have done now what he asked me to do when he gave me this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, that was when you were testifying in the Keraterm case, was it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct, yes. In the Keraterm case, yes. I must have got the dates mixed up. But in any case, I know that I found this document in my bag. I know it had been in my bag for a long time, and I had forgotten to fulfill my promise and hand it over to the Tribunal. I was not given the name of a specific person to whom to give the document. Mr. -- The gentleman who gave me this document only said: "Give it to the Tribunal." And as I was already leaving, I did this in the way I have just described.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's all I needed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just one question for clarification: On page 13, line 14 of our today's transcript, it reads: (redacted) Did I understand you correctly that you received this document by (redacted) as it reads on the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You received it from this (redacted)., as we can read the name here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I received it when he was already on his way home and had packed his things some 10 minutes before we left. He was putting his documents inside his bag, and it was then that he asked me to hand this document over to somebody at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing I'm having a quick check made of, if I can, is whether this was a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may well be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: All the time I thought about the 30 minutes rule --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- And therefore, to be on the safe side, let's redact this name from the transcript. Probably we can come back to this later. It was mentioned as I said, page 13, line 14. And then unfortunately I myself quoted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've just had it confirmed, Your Honour, he was a protected witness. If that could be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If that could be redacted immediately, starting 13:14, and then all the time this name is mentioned in the transcript, please. Please, send the pages 13 to 15 to me, and I'll take care of this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's going out on public session in the foyer, lobby, then it ought to be made sure it doesn't go out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Before we start now the continuation of the cross-examination, let me first express my gratitude that the Defence was prepared to have such enormous break during cross-examination. I know it's not facilitating your work, but we appreciate really that you consented. Thank you once again. But now it's your turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On the back of the exhibit you were reviewing, S128B, can you tell me whose handwriting appears on that page?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't pay attention to it. I see that it is handwriting, and that it's a telephone number. But I don't know. I didn't pay special attention to it. I didn't even study the document in detail when it was given to me. But when I found it in my bag at the airport, I immediately asked the gentleman called Greg to hand it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know who this individual Osman is that's referred to there, or can you read to us what it says? Because it's more than just a number. There seems to be two numbers and two names, if you would be kind enough to read that into the record for us.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can read it. On the back, there is a handwritten name, Osman, followed by the number 811-407. It could be a telephone number. Underneath it says Caus, and then the number 815-248. This is what can be seen on the back of the document. But what this means, well, the person who gave me this document would probably know if that was the person who made these notes, or if somebody else did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you would have no information as to whether this is the same Osman that we were referencing during our cross-examination who was involved with the Territorial Defence and/or the Kozarac police station. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that's so, because that person is from a different part of Prijedor. This man is from Gomjenica, or Cele, which is a completely different part of Prijedor, separate from Kozarac. So I don't think there's a connection, but I recommend that you contact this person, and he will probably know what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, going back now to your direct and cross-examination of the last couple weeks, we talked about briefly the announcement that was made on or about April 30th, 1992, at the time of the takeover in Prijedor. I'm trying to just focus you on that time. With respect to that, sir, in May of 1996, you testified that the announcement over the radio, on page 912, line 12 through 15, was as follows: "Radio Prijedor started to broadcast its announcements straight away that morning saying the SDS undertook some measures in order to debloc authority in Prijedor. The SDS members appeared on broadcast very often during the day." Similarly, sir, in your testimony sworn as it was in the Kovacevic trial on page 419, lines 21 through 25, you were asked a similar question regarding the announcements on the radio indicating who had been responsible for the takeover. You answered in the affirmative, and you continued to state: "They were quite open about it. They said that the Serbian Democratic Party had taken over all power in the municipality, so that the municipality could function normally again." In your testimony here, sir, on pages 96 and 97, you told us that you heard the announcement. And I understand that it has been several years since that time, over ten. You told us that you heard the public announcement of the Crisis Staff. In neither 1996, in your testimony in May of 1996 in the Tadic case, or your testimony in July of 1998 in the Kovacevic case did you ever, sir, mention that the Crisis Staff participated or even existed at the time when these alleged announcements were made over Radio Prijedor. And I'd like you to reconcile for us how is it that today, or recently, are you able to recall after ten years that in fact it wasn't as you stated earlier, but it was the Crisis Staff that made those announcements? Can you reconcile that for me?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the former -- previous trials, I was asked whether I had heard an announcement over the radio. I listened to that announcement, perhaps two or three times. I was not able to quote the content of the announcement, but I remember some details quite clearly, even today. Whether at the beginning of the announcement it was said that it was the Crisis Staff making the announcement, that I'm not sure of. I can't remember that. Several days ago, I was not asked specifically whether the words "Crisis Staff" had been used. I can neither confirm nor deny this. I can't remember. But the Crisis Staff was the authority that issued communiques, and that is a fact. I know that interpretations were given as to why this was done, that some people's names were mispronounced, for example, Becir Medunjanin from Kozarac was said to be called Becir Medunjani, which sounds like an Albanian last name and first name. And this was done to create among the Serbian population a feeling that this was parallel to what had been happening in Kosovo. They referred to him as Becir Medunjani, and I did pay attention to this. I noticed this. So I cannot confirm or deny who formally issued the announcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm not asking you here to give me your opinion. I'm asking you as a fact witness, as a person identified by the OTP solely as a fact witness. You tell me, sir, which is true? Was is it that the SDS made the announcements or was it this Crisis Staff that you told us a couple weeks ago that they made the announcements? Is it your testimony in 1996 and 1998 that we should believe, and is it different, and how so, from your testimony here today? And if you don't remember, simply tell us --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it's not different. It's not different. There was only one body in the municipality of Prijedor which was in power. There was the Crisis Staff, and nothing else. There was nothing above the Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff was composed of the SDS leadership, the people from the municipality from the SDS, and if I said an "SDS announcement," I meant the people who were from the SDS. Who ordered this announcement to be read, that, I don't know. I do not remember whether at the beginning of the announcement it was said that the SDS of Prijedor or the Crisis Staff were making this announcement. That, I don't remember. But I'm talking about people who belonged to a particular political party and who were appointed to certain posts, and then took over power by military means. If you're asking me about the legal issue of who made this announcement, I don't know. But I know they were SDS people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right. With respect to the name that you were just referencing, Becir, I think, Medunjanin, do you know if that was identified by a newspaper man, or who was actually distorting or misstating his name, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember who the person was, but the name was pronounced as Becir Medunjani, on several occasions. This was done persistently.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: On April or May 1st, 1992, the day after the takeover, you shared with us that you went to the town of Prijedor. At that time you said you saw that flags were hoisted, Serbian flags. Did you notice, sir, at all whether or not the flags of the -- Yugoslavian flag was hoisted as well on those same federal and republic local institutions? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw two flags. I think I saw two flags in front of the municipality. As for other buildings, I didn't see what kind of flags there were. I didn't pass by the MUP building. I saw the MUP building at a distance of about 80 metres, but I took another street. I went around it, went to the party, and from the party, I went down the main street and arrived at the municipality. As for the institutions, there was the MUP building. I don't remember what I saw on the MUP building. I just remember what I saw in front of it, from the corner from which I was looking. It's possible there was a Yugoslav flag. I think there were two flags in front of the municipality. But I don't remember that there was a Yugoslav flag with a five-pointed star. I think there was no five-pointed star on it. But I really don't remember that detail now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me understand, please, is it that you remember the Yugoslavian flag or you don't remember the flag at all but you know that there were two flags but yet you only remember the Serbian flag with the four Cs. Or do you remember that there was a Yugoslavian flag without the five-pointed star? Which one of the variations would you like us to believe?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a Yugoslav flag without a five-pointed star, and a Serbian flag, but there was no flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That had been taken down. And as far as I can recall at present, without -- without getting into the situation deeper, that's what I can remember. I think there was the Yugoslav flag without a five-pointed star, and the Serbian flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify another issue if I may, during your visits to and from Trnopolje. You went into Trnopolje yourself, and then you left Trnopolje, and then returned at a later time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How long were you there at the Trnopolje camp, physically? For how many days, nights, or any way you can quantify it for us?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot quantify this precisely. I never have been able to. I thought about it several times. I tried to remember the chronological order of events. I like to do this for myself. But as I've already said, I have lost my orientation in time, and sometimes two days seem to have lasted much longer. Or five days seemed to pass by in a flash depending on what you're experiencing at the time. What I can say with certainty is that it was between three and five days that I spent in the camp of Trnopolje. Whether it was five or three, I simply cannot tell you with any precision. Three, four, or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, which ever many days it was --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible it was three days, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Whichever way or however long it was, did you have an opportunity while you were at the Trnopolje camp to observe the people who were within that camp?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you able to, sir, see whether the people that were within that Trnopolje camp, whether they were of mixed age and gender?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were women, there were children, there were adult men. But they were separated. They could not sleep together. They were separated. That was the camp regime at the point when I arrived. 15 days before that, the regime was quite different, and the people who were there told me this, but then it was changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's try to focus your testimony on what you know, what you experienced, and what you observed. I'm sure my learned friend from the other side will ask you about all the hearsay, all the hypothetical, and all the other stuff you heard. For my purposes, I'm really interested in what you saw and observed. While at Trnopolje, is it fair to say, sir, that it was not a camp which had exclusively men of military age?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were not exclusively men of military age. These men were, however, in separate rooms, and they were grouped together. The women were accommodated in different parts of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Had anyone, sir, come to Trnopolje camp during the time that you were there, was it open and obvious for them to see people of mixed age and gender, meaning women, children, men, et cetera? Older and younger? True?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already answered this. There were people of all ages and both sexes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, was it so open and so obvious that anyone who would come there, whether it be a monitor or any other individual who happened to come along Trnopolje camp, that it was easy --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, it was not open and obvious?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From the camp, one could go out, if one had approval, with approval. People would go to the sentry posts and get approval to go and get food. That's one part of my answer. The next part of my answer is that people were brought to the camp in buses from other parts of Prijedor, from Puharska, from Rizvanovici, and some other places. Also, some people were transferred from Keraterm to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if we're understanding each other, and it might be an issue with the question that I posed to you. My question is very straightforward, sir. The Trnopolje camp, and when I say open, I'm not saying open for people to have access to come in and out. We'll discuss that. If someone were to just happen upon the camp, was it obvious to them merely to see that the camp contained people of mixed gender and age? It was rather obvious, wasn't it? It didn't take you three days to figure that out, did it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, one could see that there were both men and women there. One could see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever, sir --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least, at the point in time when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During the time that you were there, did the women leave the camp and bring food back to others within the camp? Did you observe that at all?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mostly men who went to get food after getting approval. I saw that. I saw several men getting permission to go to their houses and bring back some flour or some potatoes. And I know that several men also got permission to take a tractor or a truck and catch some stray cattle, slaughter them, and bring them back to the camp in order to provide food for the inmates. I think the person's name was Rega, but I'm not completely sure. I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Had you, sir, having lived near Trnopolje, had you been to this facility prior to April of 1992, ever?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the rooms inside the building? Yes, in some of them. So I saw some of them before, but not others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How was the camp facilities different from the time that you visited it prior to April 1992 and that which you experienced in June and July of 1992? How was the structure different, if at all?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How was it different?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If at all.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the building construction or?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Any physical attributes that you noted, sir, or observed in connection with this Trnopolje facility prior to April 30th and that which you experienced after or during June and July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were several details. Around the facility and around the stadium, there were armed soldiers and machine-gun nests. Then it was also different because the desks and chairs had been taken out of the school, and some men slept on the floor in the classrooms, at least in some of the classrooms where I spent one night. In fact, I spent one night in the corridor, but near the door of a classroom. About the other buildings, I don't know. The building across the road was a family house. At that time, it was the camp command. And the family was not living in the house any more. Commander Kuruzovic, commander Slavko, the soldiers and guards were there. There was another house where soldiers slept. There was a house belonging to a person called Hamdo, and this was also inhabited by soldiers, or at least upstairs, there were soldiers. That's what I can say about it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, that the Trnopolje camp does not and did not have either prior to April 1992 or after April of 1992, a barbed wire surrounding the entire camp? Yes or no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. The wire existed before April 1992. It existed if you look from the Trnopolje/Kozarac Road, you see it was there where the farmhouse was. And there was also another barbed wire. It was the sort of boundary from the football stadium. There was an old wire which was slightly damaged, but existed nevertheless. On the other two sides there was no barbed wire, not before, not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, sir, because you didn't itemize it as one of the descriptions that the wire that you described in connection with the stadium or the other part of the Trnopolje facility, that, in fact, that had not changed. It had been the same as you saw it prior to April 1992 as when you saw it in June and July of 1992. Correct? Same fence in the same place?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but within the barbed wires, there was something else. Instead of sandbags and other things, there were people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right. Let me ask you this: Do you know, sir, prior to April of 1992 -- first strike that. How far do you live from Trnopolje camp? How far did you live from Trnopolje camp in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I used to live perhaps 200 metres from the building, 200, 250 metres from the Trafo building or the farmer's cooperative building.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if at any time prior to April 1992, the Trnopolje facility was used for any refugees, prior to April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before April 1992. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about right after the war in Croatia? Do you know if there were any Serbian refugees that were housed in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before April, sir, the community centre was operating. The farmer's cooperative was working, the school was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you're saying that Serbian refugees were not, at any time, at the Trnopolje facility. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. There may have been a number of them, a number of Serb refugees did come to the area. It was not a large number, however, and it was not something that could be visibly seen passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can have the Court instruct the usher to show the witness Exhibit S144B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, we're going to change the topic a little bit here now and ask a couple questions on mobilisation if you don't mind. I'm going to give you this document and ask you a couple questions on that. Sir, can you tell us whether or not this was a mandatory or voluntary request for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, after the census of citizens who were at the disposal of the Territorial Defence, the TO decided to send calls and to organise. The TO may have done this before that with the regular members of the TO. I don't know. But later on, I know that on the basis of voluntary situation, they were -- there was a callup in that stage. On that list, there were people who were older, who were younger, who were subject or not subject to military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we're speaking of the mobilisation that was issued on April 8th, 1992, correct, approximately three and a half weeks before the takeover of Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the invitation, the call of the republican staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is S144 that call from the republican staff?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is the TO of the BiH and the Kozarac TO. This republican call should have gone through the municipal bodies, through the existing municipal structure, but it was not impossible to implement it, given the situation because some members were in favour and some were against. But in Kozarac, the TO structure continued to exist, and at one moment, it tried to organise mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you have an opinion, sir, as to whether or not it was successful in organising that mobilisation, in light of the fact that we showed you the document listing members of the Territorial Defence last week?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could give you my own personal view, not on the basis of my own insight into the documents. I can give you my own opinion, my own impression. I believe that the process of mobilisation had started, but was not completed because of the acceleration of events and because the military attack on Kozarac began. I think the process of mobilisation and of creating defensive forces was not fully complete before the attack on Kozarac. In some parts, yes; in some parts, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now, Your Honour, if I can have the usher show Mr. Sejmenovic Exhibit D7A and B, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My first question to you, sir, before you testified in this case and gave your written statement on June 11th, 2002, was this document one of the numerous and relevant documents the OTP asked you to review in connection with your testimony in this matter?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't -- I don't remember the Prosecution having shown me that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It only happened a couple weeks ago. You don't know that it happened or you just can't remember that it happened?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, allow me to go through the document, to skim through it, and then I shall tell you. No, I didn't see that document. I'm seeing it for the very first time. It's a document I may have seen one or two pages of that document, but I didn't see this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, help me with this, Mr. Sejmenovic: Do you think or do you have an opinion that if there's a document that has your name on it, that it would be relevant, at least for you to review? Would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's not a problem for --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think that's a question he can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, it's a question you could ask the other party, but not the witness, why. I think the answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the first page of this document on the B/C/S version, if you will, which starts I believe on the top right-hand corner, page 328. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, the date of this document seems to be the 30th of April, 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says: "April 30th, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you could just take a look at that first page, sir, do you know any of the individuals that are mentioned there such as Beco, Islam, Melkic, Sivac, Nagib, Medic, Osman, Suljo, Kemo Fazlic? Do you recognise any of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise some of them, Beco may have been Becir Medunjanin. Islam, Islam Bahonjic perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's not guess. Let's look at the lower part of that page where it gives their first and last name, under the word delegation.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Well, sir, you showed me the beginning of the document. You should have told me to see the end of the page, too. We have the name Fazlic --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Sejmenovic. I'm only pointing to where you can find that. It's not a criticism. Please don't take it as a criticism. Do you know those individuals who are listed on that page?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Islam Bahonjic, Becir Medunjanin. I know Ilijaz Memic. The name here is Ilko, but I suppose it's Ilijaz. Kemal Fazlic. I know there was a person by that name in Kozarac. But I don't believe I know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what this document is, at least this first page that you've had an opportunity to look at?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, may I first read it, and then tell you? I see that it is a minutes, a record. It is written by hand. I don't know what it addresses. Is it written by a body, whether it is a minutes from a meeting? I don't know. I can only read what is written in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, help me with this: On the first thing, Beco talks about a main road issue. Do you have any idea what he's referring to, sir, in that first paragraph? Or maybe you could read the first paragraph to us if you would be kind enough, out loud.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not very legible, at least the first part. I'll try to read it slowly. "Beco-Prijedor. Prijedor cannot help us at all. State of mobility," well, this cannot be read. Then the word "population, not to undertake measures aimed at provocation." This part is also illegible. Then it says: "Which Miskovic stated in an angry voice." I think that is what it says. Then "to establish contact with party in the municipality, the state of the main road." It is not legible. You can see for yourself. The copy is not legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have it, thank you. What main road issue, if you know, were they discussing, sir, or the state of the main road? What is it that they are discussing there, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be sure. I know that the Banja Luka/Prijedor Road was referred to a highway, sometimes do not consider to be a main road. But if the records are correct, if it is something from a meeting, that it may refer to that road, the Prijedor/Kozarac Road or the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road. I cannot give you an exact answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this: Do you know what they are talking about when they state "not to undertake actions with the aim of provoking?" Did you ever have any discussions with these individuals about an issue of provocation by the Muslims against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the general attitude. Much energy was invested in this. And theoretically, one could not give occasion, a motivation, for the Serb Army to attack. We knew it practice that it provoked but then blamed the other side and began attacking. And that's why we had to be additionally cautious.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this: From April 30th through May 22nd, 1992, which is the date I think we've earmarked as the incident occurring on Hambarine, and then the attack, if you dispute that, just share it with us, but we have that as an approximation, but during that time period, sir, were there any attacks by the military to any Bosnian Muslim village or territory during that time period, from April 30th through May 22nd, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were attacks in other parts of Bosnia. We heard about those events on television, in Zvornik, in Bijeljina, in Bosanski Novi. We listened to this information and it was always the Serb side. The Banja Luka television kept saying that the Serb army had been attacked and that it was compelled to respond by bringing units to Bosnian towns. And in Croatia, and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was the civilians or the other side that attacked the Serb army, and then the attack began. This was a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Or an attack by the military or the police or civilians on any Bosnian Muslim communities or homes from the period of April 30th, 1992, up to including and May 22nd, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I know that in Trnopolje, they were firing at non-Serb from the Ribnjak area, at non-Serb homes. This happened on several occasions, even before the takeover. Well, I can give you specific names of the peoples who owned these homes. I can --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry to interrupt, can I just have clarification because I'm not clear from the question that was asked, was the question were there any attacks anywhere in Bosnia or just limited to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It was certainly limited to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Because it wasn't clear from the way the question came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The second one I think was, but the first one he answered in a little more broad sense, not to direct --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I heard the question, that whether anywhere in Bosnia in those days there were attacks, and I answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You're correct. We're not debating that.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you are claiming that there was no such question, that you hadn't asked that question. Then perhaps there may have been a translation problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... That was the question. Is it the question of the question -- I'm sorry, it is the witness's knowledge that he's seeking or whether there were actually attacks elsewhere? Because there's a difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We know there's a difference because we've heard his testimony ad nauseum about the difference between the two. If counsel has an objection, state it, give a basis, and if I feel it's appropriate before the Court rules, I'll restate my question. If I disagree, the Court will rule, and depending on the ruling I'll either restate it or ask a different question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stands adjourned until ten minutes past 4.00. Probably the parties can then in the meantime agree on the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before cross-examination continues, we've seen the orders. Would Your Honour grant some time either at the end of today or tomorrow afternoon before the hearing so that I can raise two matters that arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whichever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We'll come back to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could the witness please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could the witness please expect the questions of the Defence counsel before answering. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, prior to the break, you mentioned that you did hear of some instances in the Bosnia-Herzegovina area in connection with massacres, provocation, et cetera. And my question truly was initially confined to the Prijedor area, but you answered in the general. And since you answer that way, I just have a follow-up. Since you did hear about these instances of either attacks, or however we want to categorise them, did you sir at any time hear about the massacre or the killings at Sijekovac or Kupres? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me whether I heard and whether there were any attacks by the army on the population anywhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina. After that, you said you hadn't asked me that. And I wanted to say that you had. I answered you that I heard about this from the media. We had reports from the Sarajevo television. We could watch it sometimes, and we could listen to Radio Sarajevo all the time. At the same time, we had information from the same events from the Banja Luka television. There were clashes between the JNA and the population in Kupres, in Sarajevo, in Tuzla. But you asked me about army attacks on the non-Serbian population, and that's what my reply was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you did hear about Kupres. Did you hear about Sijekovac? The incidents involving that, or the massacre that occurred in Sijekovac. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard of Sijekovac, but I can't remember exactly what happened. I know there were a lot of news reports on the events on Kupres, the attempted exercises by the Yugoslav Army which turned into something else. There were armed conflicts, but I don't know any details about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me confine my question, then, sir, with respect to the Prijedor municipality, is it true that there were no attacks by the military or police on any Muslim homes or territories within the Prijedor municipality from April 30th, 1992, up until the incident that we've exhaustively discussed at times, May 22nd, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about there were some shootings. Did you hear, sir, of the policeman that was shot, the Serbian policeman that was shot on May 2nd, 1992, in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you have already asked me. This I know that there were some information on the radio about this, but I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any details as to who the person was that shot the Serbian policeman? Do you recall the details regarding that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I've already said that I don't know any details about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to Document Defence Exhibit 7A and B. And we're still on this first page which has the date on the top centre of the 30th of April, 1992. Sir, do you know what this delegation was that was formed and that met on or about April 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't give you a precise answer to this. I know that there were several delegations in that period, and that we tried to send delegations to Prijedor and to Banja Luka, to try to talk to the government of the autonomous region and agree on peace in the area. And also, with a representatives of the authorities in Prijedor. So I can't be sure about this delegation. Perhaps it was this delegation that went to negotiate in Prijedor, but from what it says here, I really can't tell you what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Turning to the next page on your document, which has on the top right-hand corner page 346, and for our purposes, on the English version, it starts on the bottom of the first page, 377, sir, that's a document that is dated the 2nd of May, 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, it says here the 2nd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the individual is by the name of Nagib who appears after the third item on the agenda, "miscellaneous," is referred to? Do you know who that individual is?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who Nagib is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It states here, sir, at least from the English translation, and I'd invite you to read the Serbian one that "a lot of --" I mean the B/C/S one. "A lot of our people carry out attacks of provocation, Fazlic and Hasan, and Didin yesterday fired in order to provoke." And it goes on to say: "The police should immediately take such people to the police station and disarm them." You told us many times during your testimony that you were and would have been informed of certain instances that occurred in the Prijedor Municipality. Were you, sir, at time informed that "a lot of our people carry out attacks of provocation"? Were you informed of that at any time, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm listening to the interpretation of what you're saying, and looking at the original text, and in the interpretation, the meaning is quite different. I will read, and perhaps we will have a better interpretation the other way around into English. It says here: --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doesn't it say Puno, sir? Does it say Puno?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Puno, okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Hold on. I'd only ask you if you ask the B/C/S version, instead of interpreting it --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I quote, I quote. I quote: "A lot of our people are carrying out provocations." You said "are carrying out provocative attacks, which is something quite different. Further it says: "Fazlic and Hasan Didin yesterday fired shots on their own initiative as the police arrests and disarms these immediately." I can tell you at that time, anywhere it was forbidden to fire shots anywhere, whether in front of your own house or anywhere else. There were no front lines, no military formations on the ground, and it was simply not possible to carry out provocative attacks, which is what you said. I am trying to clarify for Their Honours and for you what this is about. There was a firm decision that any attempts to fire shots should be punished, whether this took place in a cafe, in the street, in front of one's house, or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that acts of provocation were being committed by people such as Fazlic, Hasan, and Didin?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in the town, in Kozarac, that some people were arrested, and the police confiscated weapons from some people because they fired shots in cafes or in front of their houses when they were drunk, and the police punished this wherever they could. I know about this phenomenon. This did not occur frequently. It was not widespread. But any kind of shooting was immediately punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, partake in any of the hearings or investigation that led to the punishment of these individuals who were carrying out acts of provocation? Were you intimately involved in that at all?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended several meetings, and I have already mentioned this, in Kozarac. We know what the duty of the police was, and we know what the police were supposed to do. I also know that some people were arrested and disarmed. These people were drunk. I was not an eyewitness, but if a police chief arrived and said, "in front of the cafe, we did this and that," I had no reason not to believe him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know the individual who is identified on this date as Suljo, and below I think you'll find his last name, I believe, Kozarusa. Do you know Suljo Kozarusa?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Kozarusa is a last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It could mean that he's Suljo from Kozarusa. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could mean that, yes. That Suljo is from Kozarusa, but I can't remember who that person might be, Suljo from Kozarusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have any understanding of what the discussion regarding the BH TO insignia was, and why there would be a misunderstanding with the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. army?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At party meetings, and the meetings of the municipal functionaries who were not allowed to work in the municipal organs, there were many discussions as to what standpoint we should take, how we should try to solve this problem and protect the population from an attack by the Serbian Army. Many options were discussed. If the Court is interested in this, I can speak of it in greater detail. There were many proposals that all these functionaries should meet outside the territory, and that the municipal organs should be set up somewhere else. There were also proposals that none of this should be done, but that we should simply retain the status quo. There were also proposals that regardless of the negotiations, because there was an evident threat, we should start preparing to defend the population. There were also crazy proposals such as writing a letter to the United Nations because we had no connections with Sarajevo and so on and so forth. So there was a whole range of proposals, but ultimately it all boiled down to the fact that the existing institutions should be put at the service of organising the defence, and that all potential should be directed at trying to reach an agreement with the Serbian side, that delegations should be sent to Banja Luka and to Prijedor. We used people's personal connections with Serbian functionaries in Prijedor and Banja Luka. Every means was explored to try to establish contact. That was the process that was taking place. There were also proposals that a new municipality should be established, but this was not adopted. It remained just a proposal. There were also many discussions as to how the Territorial Defence should be organised and extended because technically, the capacity was nonexistent. The headquarters of the Territorial Defence and all the records were in Prijedor. So how could we organise a Territorial Defence without provoking an attack? Simply by organising it. This was a very complex situation, and we were looking for the best way to protect the population and to avoid giving a pretext to the Serbian side for an attack. This whole process was going on at the time. Another thing, at the time there were Serbs from Kozarac who were members of these groups that discussed these matters. They were from Trnopolje, from Kozarusa, I think there were also some from Gornji Jakupovici. So it was not an ethnically pure or single -- it was not a group coming from a -- coming from a single ethnic group. So some of these Serbs were included in the delegations I'm speaking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is, I don't have an understanding of the insignia and how it can avoid or how there could be a misunderstanding with the army. On that quote, from Suljo from Kozarusa, my question to you, sir, is which army is he referring to, and what is the misunderstanding that he's having with the insignia that the BH TO was creating?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suljo Kozarusa, I quote: "We reject for now the insignia of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to avoid disagreements with the army." At that time, that is, on the 2nd of May, 1992, the Yugoslav army still officially existed in this area. And this is in line with what I have been saying. We wanted to avoid the fact that we were organising to prevent it from provoking the army, so one of the proposals was to reject the insignia of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But things were happening very fast. There were no uniforms; there was nothing. I know that people asked the civilian protection to give them clothing which could be adapted for the Territorial Defence. And of course, there were no insignia. But this was a standpoint because the Yugoslav army still existed at the time and did not recognise the Territorial Defence in Kozarac, but only the Territorial Defence that had placed itself under their command in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You state, sir, that there were no uniforms, but doesn't Suljo several lines down also tell us that "you're getting the uniforms on Monday," several days later?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have just explained part of this. The regular Territorial Defence numbered a very small number of men. We extended it. I don't know the exact number, but it was perhaps 2 or 3.000 men. I don't know the exact number because I wasn't part of it. I know that at the meetings, we discussed the problem of how to clothe these men. Otherwise, they would be in T-shirts, jackets if there was an attack. So then they asked the firefighters to give them their reserve uniforms, and then the civilian protection, which had blue overalls, and also blue workers' overalls from a company. And it was agreed that these should be dyed so that the greatest number of possible people would have uniforms. Preparations for this was made but whether this was actually carried out, I don't know. I know that these uniforms never arrived in the area of Trnopolje where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know the gentleman by the name of Kenjar and the last name starting with the letter "S?" Do you know the individual identified on May 2nd, 1992, as Kenjar with the last name "S"? Or it could be actually his last name is Kenjar and his first name starts with the letter "S".

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kenjar, it must be Sakib Kenjar from Kamicani, probably. I remember a person called Sakib Kenjar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what his role was on or about April and May of 1992 in either Kozara or in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the municipal board of the SDA, and I think for a time, he was the treasurer or the secretary. I'm not sure. But in any case, he was on the municipal board and of the local board of the Kamicani SDA. He was a member of the Executive Board for a time, I just remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It states here in part that Mr. Kenjar states in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you slow down a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- "Some guys are provoking too much." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. "Some guys in Kozarac are provoking too much."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I assume he's referring to the same people as the previous person you asked me about, Nagib or whatever his name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Also whatever on that date, Beco Medunjanin, he states that they were preparing the units possibly or maybe for inspection. Do you see that? He's the second one after Nagib, under Suljo.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beco says here: "I checked about Muharem, and it was Enes Grcin who fired shots. Improve organisation so as not to overburden the men." The issue of insignia, let's wait a little and prepare the units. Maybe for the inspection."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what -- can you tell me again who this Beco was, what his function or capacity was on or about May 2nd, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I have to restate the question, Mr. Sejmenovic. Can you tell me who this Beco was and what his function and capacity was on or about May 2nd, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the secretary of the secretariat of defence. So he was -- he held a post in the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you, sir, have any idea what units he was talking about when he said he "should prepare the units for inspection"?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the units of the Territorial Defence, well, that was his department. He was in charge of the Territorial Defence and carrying out the mobilisation. That was his function before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who was to conduct the inspection?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commanders of the Territorial Defence, if there was an inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On the next page of this same date, yours page 345; for the English translation, it appears on page 325 on the top right-hand corner, there's an Avdo who makes a statement regarding - somewhat illegible - regarding the receiving of two machine-guns and two automatic rifles. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know or can you make out from whom did Avdo receive these two machine-guns and two automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe from other local communes, or maybe they were bought from Serbs. But in any case, it was according to the Territorial Defence establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Suljo on May 2nd, 1992, states: "If Kozarusa does not receive help, it will surrender all the checkpoints." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many checkpoints were there in Kozarusa on or about May 2nd, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
